c.tagline: Cobblestone old town, golden Pacific beaches, and Mexico's most welcoming beach city on the Bay of Banderas.

taxi.fareNote: Puerto Vallarta taxis are not metered — agree the fare before getting in, as drivers charge by zone. Uber and DiDi both operate and are usually cheaper, though taxi unions restrict app pickups at some spots like the airport and Marina.

emergency.note: 911 is Mexico's unified emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance; 078 is the national tourist assistance line, and Puerto Vallarta has a dedicated tourist police force.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.El Centro (Malecón): Malecon Puerto Vallarta Our Lady of Guadalupe

avoid.reason: Tourist zone safe; caution downtown at night; avoid drug involvement (cartel presence)

hood_desc: The lively heart of Puerto Vallarta's tourism south of the Cuale River, centered on Los Muertos Beach, the Basilio Badillo 'Restaurant Row,' and Olas Altas; it's the walkable hub of the city's dining, bars, and famously vibrant LGBTQ+ nightlife.

The historic downtown north of the river along the oceanfront Malecón boardwalk, home to the Church of Our Lady of Guadalupe, sculpture-lined promenades, art galleries, and the main plaza; best for first-timers who want sights, street life, and cobblestone charm.

A planned upscale resort district around a yacht-filled marina north of downtown, with a golf course, waterfront restaurants, condos, and big-brand hotels; suits travelers wanting a calm, self-contained base near the airport.

The strip of large beachfront resort hotels lining the bay between downtown and the Marina; a convenient, low-key all-inclusive base with easy beach access, though it lacks the character of the old town.

An exclusive hillside neighborhood just south of the Romantic Zone with dramatic bay views, secluded rocky coves, and luxury villas and boutique hotels; suits couples and travelers wanting a quiet, scenic, upscale retreat.
lodging: Almar Resort Luxury LGBT Beach Front Experience

water.note: The city certifies its municipal supply, but nearly everyone drinks bottled or purified water.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5:00am to 11:00pm along the main Highway 200 corridor; water taxis run in daylight hours. Late-night travel relies on taxis or ride apps.
transit.note: There is no metro, tram, or rail; getting around means cheap urban buses along the bay, taxis, ride-hail apps, or water taxis from the Los Muertos and Boca de Tomatlán piers to the roadless southern-shore beaches.
transit.pay: City buses ('camiones') are paid in cash to the driver, about MXN 10-12 (~US$0.60) per ride; there is no rechargeable transit card. Buses are marked by destination (Centro, Marina, Tunel, Aeropuerto) and run the main corridors. Water taxis to southern beaches like Yelapa and Las Ánimas are paid in cash at the pier.
